[{:db/id 17592186240891 :question/worked-solution "First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=3-\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{3-\text{i}}=3+\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(3-\text{i}+(3+\text{i)})x+(3-\text{i})(3+\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+({3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+10 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-6x+10$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x+2 \\  & {x}^{2}-6x+10\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-\phantom{2}2x+20} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+10x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,2{x}^{2}-12x+20 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{2{x}^{2}-12x+20}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

     

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-6x+10)(x+2).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2=0\,⟹\,x=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=-2,3\pm \text{i}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186240892 :question/worked-solution "First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116.$

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-5+2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-5+2\text{i}}=-5-2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(-5+2\text{i}+(-5-2\text{i)})x+(-5+2\text{i})(-5-2\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+((-5)^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+29 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+10x+29$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x-4 \\  & {x}^{2}+10x+29\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}+\phantom{1}6{x}^{2}-11x-116} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+10{x}^{2}+29x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,-4{x}^{2}+40x-116 \\  & \,\,\,{-4{x}^{2}+40x-116}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

        

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+10x+29)(x-4).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=4,-5\pm 2\text{i}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186399982 :question/problem "![](images/37/37434a61262f829160fc2b19fcadb67745a024d589cd1ce318ca4ab90d6ab2d9.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y=\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}}$ that is closest to the point $(2,0)$ satisfies the equation

$$
2x-3-\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186266081 :question/problem "The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${A}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186401364 :question/problem "The domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=2{t}^{3}\,i+(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,k$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \bbox[5pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}.
$$

What is the missing expression? You may assume that $n$ is an integer." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186401378 :question/problem "The domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=(1-{t}^{3})\,i+3\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,k$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \bbox[5pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}.
$$

What is the missing expression? You may assume that $n$ is an integer." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186284691 :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)={x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-12x-16.$ Since ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ are roots of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem, 

$$
(x+1)(x-4)={x}^{2}-3x-4
$$

is a factor of $f(x).$ 

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-3x-4$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{x}^{2}+4 \\  & {x}^{2}-3x-4\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}\phantom{+0x}\,\,\,-12x-16\,\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,4{x}^{2}-12x-16 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{4{x}^{2}-12x-16}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-3x-4)({x}^{2}+4).$

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}+4=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =-4 \\ x & =\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-1,\,4,\,\pm 2\text{i}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186299700 :question/problem "The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${B}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[B\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186403011 :question/problem "![](images/47/47849c87c3c8cf9008b6531e740c6fc57058905cf17e31e4c93c479f337f0fbd.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y={e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ that is closest to the point $(1,0)$ satisfies the equation

$$
2x-2+\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186403947 :question/problem "Consider a system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables, written in matrix form as $D\,z=c.$ Here, $D$ is the non-singular coefficient matrix of the system, $z$ is the column vector containing the variables, and $c$ is the column vector containing the constants. The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & =\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{D}^{-1}}}}c \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{I}_{n}}}}z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

From top to bottom and right to left, what are the missing parts of the derivation?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186403954 :question/problem "Consider a system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables, written in matrix form as $D\,t=q.$ Here, $D$ is the non-singular coefficient matrix of the system, $t$ is the column vector containing the variables, and $q$ is the column vector containing the constants. The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,t & =q \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{D}^{-1}}}}D\,t & ={D}^{-1}\,q \\ {I}_{n}\,t & ={D}^{-1}\,\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{\mathbf{q}}}} \\ t & ={D}^{-1}\,q\end{aligned}
$$

From top to bottom and left to right, what are the missing parts of the derivation?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]}]

equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}y+2z=0 \\ x+2y+3z=2 \\ 3x+y+z=-3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186092187 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186092027 :question/id #uuid "06a50eb4-4976-55fd-aa44-6509b27eccb9" $$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider a system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables, written in matrix form as $D\,t=q.$ Here, $D$ is the non-singular coefficient matrix of the system, $t$ is the column vector containing the variables, and $q$ is the column vector containing the constants. The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$

$$

$$

$$
{A}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].

\begin{aligned}[B\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${B}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{B}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186329703 :question/id #uuid "d7c177d5-936c-5b91-b2dd-2e563024c669" :question/math-academy-id "q-42987"} {:db/id 17592186329705 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, we let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20.$ 

Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=3-\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{3-\text{i}}=3+\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(3-\text{i}))(x-(3+\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(3-\text{i}+(3+\text{i)})x+(3-\text{i})(3+\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+({3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}-6x+10 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-6x+10$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x+2 \\  & {x}^{2}-6x+10\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+20} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+10x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,2{x}^{2}-12x+20 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{2{x}^{2}-12x+20}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

     

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-6x+10)(x+2).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2=0\,⟹\,x=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=-2,3\pm \text{i}.$"} {:db/id 17592186240892 :question/id #uuid "d1be54b7-7530-59ba-90a4-e2866a7b30e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-104516" :knowledge-point/_questions Since $f(x)$ has real coefficients and ${x}_{1}=-5+2\text{i}$ is a root of $f(x),$ the complex conjugate 

$$
\overset{―}{{x}_{1}}=\overset{―}{-5+2\text{i}}=-5-2\text{i}
$$

must also be a root of $f(x).$

Now, according to the factor theorem, 
$(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i}))$
is a factor of $f(x).$ Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-(-5+2\text{i}))(x-(-5-2\text{i})) & = \\ {x}^{2}-(-5+2\text{i}+(-5-2\text{i)})x+(-5+2\text{i})(-5-2\text{i}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+((-5)^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}) & = \\ {x}^{2}+10x+29 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}+10x+29$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,x-4 \\  & {x}^{2}+10x+29\,\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-11x-116} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{3}+10{x}^{2}+29x}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,-4{x}^{2}+40x-116 \\  & \,\,\,{-4{x}^{2}+40x-116}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

        

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}+10x+29)(x-4).$ 

To find the remaining root, we set the linear factor equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4=0\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the roots are $x=4,-5\pm 2\text{i}.$"} {:db/id 17592186244076 :question/id #uuid "18336512-5937-539b-bd8f-2d38ab91c85a" :question/math-academy-id "q-107548"} {:db/id 17592186299666 :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)={x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-12x-16.$ Since ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ are roots of $f(x),$ then according to the factor theorem, 

$$
(x+1)(x-4)={x}^{2}-3x-4
$$

is a factor of $f(x).$ 

Next, we find the quotient when $f(x)$ is divided by ${x}^{2}-3x-4$ using polynomial division.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{x}^{2}+4 \\  & {x}^{2}-3x-4\,\enclose{longdiv}{\,\,{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}\,\,\,-12x-16\,\,} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{{x}^{4}-3{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,4{x}^{2}-12x-16 \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{4{x}^{2}-12x-16}_{―} \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $f(x)=({x}^{2}-3x-4)({x}^{2}+4).$

To find the remaining two roots, we solve ${x}^{2}+4=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =-4 \\ x & =\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to our original equation are $x=-1,\,4,\,\pm 2\text{i}.$"} {:db/id 17592186299912 :question/id #uuid "d08e4df3-3ff4-5343-a353-88cc7cdc23e7" :question/math-academy-id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/37/37434a61262f829160fc2b19fcadb67745a024d589cd1ce318ca4ab90d6ab2d9.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y=\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}}$ that is closest to the point $(2,0)$ satisfies the equation

$$
2x-3-\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAA}}=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{(\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}})}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+\frac{{x}^{2}+2x+1}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x+2+\frac{1}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+\frac{1}{x}+6.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186403011 :question/id #uuid "eb0ef12c-9b61-582b-acd5-7493f7def056" :question/math-academy-id "q-49054" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198246 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "38bfb48e-9b66-58a8-966a-fb6938e08073" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Equation That Determines a Minimum Distance"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30d03c60-3151-59b6-b7b9-fd72aa928ebd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186403013} {:answer/id #uuid "5f900a01-8dad-54ab-bb5e-4a84ad557187" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{x}{sin}^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186403014} {:answer/id #uuid "a782534b-97b6-5072-b2d6-441797eca761" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186403015} {:answer/id #uuid "8cc1f314-0209-5118-9c75-ea26340d8758" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186403016} {:answer/id #uuid "704fb728-1e9d-5aae-b2b0-2c48902cd828" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186403017}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "a782534b-97b6-5072-b2d6-441797eca761" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186403015} :answer-field/id #uuid "606ee288-277b-5ad8-a08e-806ce45db66b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186403012}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/47/47849c87c3c8cf9008b6531e740c6fc57058905cf17e31e4c93c479f337f0fbd.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y={e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ that is closest to the point $(1,0)$ satisfies the equation

$$
2x-2+=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{({e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-2+{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ 2x-2+{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198247 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198080 :question/id #uuid "4b55bd03-c8ad-55b2-a51e-7f875d382627" :question/math-academy-id "e-12597"} :knowledge-point/id [{:db/id 17592186176919 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177019 :tutorial/content "The fundamental theorem of algebra tells us that any quartic polynomial with real coefficients has precisely four roots. 

Moreover, since complex roots always come in complex conjugate pairs, if $p(x)$ is a quartic polynomial with real coefficients, we must have one of the following cases:

- $p(x)$ has $4$ real roots (some of which might be repeated).

- $p(x)$ has $2$ (possibly repeated) real roots and $2$ complex conjugate roots. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & ={x}^{4}-1 \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =(x-1)(x+1)(x-\text{i})(x+\text{i}).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the real roots are $x=\pm 1,$ and the complex conjugate roots are $x=\pm\textrm i.$

- $p(x)$ has two pairs of complex conjugate roots. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)({x}^{2}+4) \\  & =(x-\text{i})(x+\text{i})(x-\text{2}\text{i})(x+\text{2}\text{i}).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the complex conjugate pairs of roots are $x=\pm\textrm i$ and $x=\pm 2\textrm i.$ 

 Also, notice that it's possible for the complex conjugate pairs of roots to be repeated. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & ={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{2} \\  & ={((x-\text{i})(x+\text{i}))}^{2} \\  & =(x-\text{i})(x-\text{i})(x+\text{i})(x+\text{i}).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the roots are $x=\pm\textrm i.$ Each of these roots is a double root." :tutorial/id #uuid "e5351df4-0c57-5a7a-96da-a70b16eecb4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5613 :tutorial/title :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186116133 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116498 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the inverse of the matrix 

![](images/fd/fd9e9dc44e27810ef490a898a7c82ae9296eaf85ac9406cf310afe86638f71e1.svg) 

We can compute the inverse of $A$ using elementary row operations. There are two key advantages to using row operations to compute the inverse of a matrix:

- The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

- It requires significantly less computation than some alternative methods. This is especially true for large matrices.

Here, we'll focus on the $2\times 2$ case. We use the following fact:

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

So, to find the inverse of $A,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}A$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
![](images/e5/e553bcc265698432452c8d35b79fe9dc70c25010a0bcc6874ad0302ea7033ed7.svg)

**Step 2:** Apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,{I}_{2}\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\,I\,|\,{A}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $A^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

![](images/b7/b7c08e9a28ebfe456a9d77ccdaf6688893dfd04ba755a989a417c8a43e80ee0c.svg)

We can easily check our result by computing $AA^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc38ae42-2cd4-53df-9ad5-568d8e3b5fd4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3167 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8efc5ed-eaaf-514d-b03a-248df406a7d5" :step/math-academy-id ![](images/fd/fd9e9dc44e27810ef490a898a7c82ae9296eaf85ac9406cf310afe86638f71e1.svg) 

We can compute the inverse of $A$ using elementary row operations. There are two key advantages to using row operations to compute the inverse of a matrix:

- The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

- It requires significantly less computation than some alternative methods. This is especially true for large matrices.

Here, we'll focus on the $2\times 2$ case. We use the following fact:

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

So, to find the inverse of $A,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}A$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
![](images/e5/e553bcc265698432452c8d35b79fe9dc70c25010a0bcc6874ad0302ea7033ed7.svg)

**Step 2:** Apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,{I}_{2}\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\,I\,|\,{A}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $A^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

![](images/b7/b7c08e9a28ebfe456a9d77ccdaf6688893dfd04ba755a989a417c8a43e80ee0c.svg)

We can easily check our result by computing $AA^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc38ae42-2cd4-53df-9ad5-568d8e3b5fd4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3167 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186116136 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115251 :question/math-academy-id "q-10091" :question/problem "Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}y+2z=0 \\ x+2y+3z=2 \\ 3x+y+z=-3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "100a637e-a49a-5d4a-80d2-e88a9e19ca4c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415693}} {:db/id 17592186415692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348099 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6788781d-31d5-5bd7-b27b-68afaa4d9325" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=B\,d\,A" :db/id 17592186346254} {:answer/id #uuid "9bded5b5-b83d-570e-9629-cd29113e20b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=B\,d\,{A}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186346708} {:answer/id #uuid "a4a497d7-ea8a-5a5f-b4fd-1d8c483ff5a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={A}^{-1}B\,d" :db/id 17592186346783} {:answer/id #uuid "b6d2cc68-86a2-5604-8401-931a07c9e6b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=BA\,d" :db/id 17592186346945} {:answer/id #uuid "e304282a-e8e7-5d48-b8b7-fb2bbc3eab5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=AB\,d" :db/id 17592186347347}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347347} :answer-field/id #uuid "b4e01459-2873-55b9-8f7c-c4fb473002de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5f0cd9e3-58c9-5ff5-838e-38f22a6e88cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-78570" :question/problem "Consider a matrix equation ${A}^{-1}\,x=B\,d,$ where $A$ and $B$ are $7\times 7$ non-singular matrices, while $x$ and $d$ are $7\times 1$ column vectors. The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & =c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

From top to bottom and right to left, what are the missing parts of the derivation?" :question/worked-solution "Since $D$ is not singular, it must have an inverse ${D}^{-1}.$ Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation $D\,z=c$ by ${D}^{-1},$ we obtain the following:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}y+2z=0 \\ x+2y+3z=2 \\ 3x+y+z=-3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "100a637e-a49a-5d4a-80d2-e88a9e19ca4c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415693}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-78559" :question/problem "Consider a system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables, written in matrix form as $D\,z=c.$ Here, $D$ is the non-singular coefficient matrix of the system, $z$ is the column vector containing the variables, and $c$ is the column vector containing the constants. The unique solution of the system can be found using the method shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & =c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

From top to bottom and right to left, what are the missing parts of the derivation?" :question/worked-solution "Since $D$ is not singular, it must have an inverse ${D}^{-1}.$ Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation $D\,z=c$ by ${D}^{-1},$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & ={D}^{-1}c \\ {I}_{n}\,z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

:tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to find the shortest distance between a point and a curve. 

For example, let's find the smallest distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1$ and the point $(5,1),$ shown below.

![](images/dc/dc1f5b350025a0fd0530531cfc887c148459194afe209e472701054c128f1079.png)

To solve this problem, we follow three steps:

**Step 1.** Use the distance formula to create a function $S(x,y)$ representing the *squared* distance between $(5,1)$ and a general point $P(x, y){:}$

$$
S = (x-5)^2 + (y-1)^2
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+25.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Calculate the first derivative $S'(x)$ and solve $S'(x) = 0$ to find the stationary point(s).

Computing the derivative $S'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{'}(x) & =2x-8.\end{aligned}
$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where $S'(x) = 0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{'}(x) & =0 \\ 2x-8 & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Use the first or second derivative tests to confirm that the stationary point minimizes the squared distance.

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
S''(4) = 2.
$$

17592186199508 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to find the shortest distance between a point and a curve. 

For example, let's find the smallest distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1$ and the point $(5,1),$ shown below.

![](images/dc/dc1f5b350025a0fd0530531cfc887c148459194afe209e472701054c128f1079.png)

To solve this problem, we follow three steps:

**Step 1.** Use the distance formula to create a function $S(x,y)$ representing the *squared* distance between $(5,1)$ and a general point $P(x, y){:}$

$$
S = (x-5)^2 + (y-1)^2
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+25.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Calculate the first derivative $S'(x)$ and solve $S'(x) = 0$ to find the stationary point(s).

Computing the derivative $S'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{'}(x) & =2x-8.\end{aligned}
$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where $S'(x) = 0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{'}(x) & =0 \\ 2x-8 & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Use the first or second derivative tests to confirm that the stationary point minimizes the squared distance.

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
S''(4) = 2.
$$

Since $S''(4) > 0,$ the point $x=4$ is a minimum of $S(x)$ by the second derivative test.

Therefore, we conclude that the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $x = 4.$ 

Finally, since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=4$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(4)} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}-8(4)+25} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ef45dd95-3bca-5734-a692-3cebc9f37432" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7893 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "25198a50-d410-5851-a1cc-00f60435537f" :step/math-academy-id 119264 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199028}} {:db/id 17592186199508 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to find the shortest distance between a point and a curve.

17592186045417] [17592186046658 1005 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning 17592186046982 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating - The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-5)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x})^{2} \\  & =(x-5)^{2}+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+25+2x \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+25.\end{aligned}

$$
S''(4) = 2.
